title: Der Dreschflegel vom Himmel
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 112. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, fieng, Thor, Noth).
about: KHM 112 is a Lügenmärchen, a tall tale told with a perfectly straight face: a farmer's ox horns grow so enormous that a butcher pays for them by the grain of rapeseed, one of which sprouts a stalk reaching all the way to heaven. The farmer climbs it, finds threshers at work up there, and has to improvise a rope of chaff to get back down — bringing along a flail as physical proof that the whole story is true.

sentences.t: Es zog einmal ein Bauer mit einem Paar Ochsen zum Pflügen aus.
sentences.l: Once a farmer set out with a pair of oxen to the ploughing.
sentences.i: A farmer once set out with a pair of oxen to plough.
sentences.n: The dummy subject “es” fills the front slot again (“Es zog einmal ein Bauer …”), and “einmal” marks this as a tale. “zog … aus” is separable ausziehen, ‘to set out,’ with the particle held to the very end. “zum Pflügen” is an infinitive used as a noun.

sentences.t: Als er auf den Acker kam, da fiengen den beiden Thieren die Hörner an zu wachsen, wuchsen fort, und als er nach Haus wollte, waren sie so groß, daß er nicht mit zum Thor hinein konnte.
sentences.l: When he came onto the field, the horns began growing on the two beasts, grew on, and when he wanted homeward, they were so big that he could not get in through the gate with them.
sentences.i: When he came to the field the two beasts’ horns began to grow, and went on growing, and when he wanted to go home they were so big that he could not get in at the gate with them.
sentences.n: “den beiden Thieren die Hörner” is the dative of possession — literally ‘to the two beasts the horns,’ where English says ‘the beasts’ horns.’ “fiengen … an” is separable anfangen in the 1857 -ie- spelling (modern fingen an). “als er nach Haus wollte”: wollen alone carries the motion, ‘wanted to go home.’ “Thieren” and “Thor” keep the 1857 -th- (modern Tieren, Tor).

sentences.t: Zu gutem Glück kam gerade ein Metzger daher, dem überließ er sie,
sentences.l: By good fortune a butcher came along just then, to whom he made them over,
sentences.i: As luck would have it, a butcher came along just then, and he let him have them,
sentences.n: “dem überließ er sie” fronts the relative pronoun — ‘to that one he made them over’ — a loose joining that English usually turns into ‘and … him.’ “Zu gutem Glück” is fixed: ‘by good luck.’

sentences.t: und schlossen sie den Handel dergestalt, daß er sollte dem Metzger ein Maß Rübsamen bringen, der wollt ihm dann für jedes Korn einen brabanter Thaler aufzählen.
sentences.l: and they struck the bargain in such wise that he should bring the butcher a measure of rape-seed, and he would then count out to him a Brabant thaler for every grain.
sentences.i: and they struck the bargain on these terms: he was to bring the butcher a measure of rapeseed, and the butcher would then count him out a Brabant thaler for every single grain.
sentences.n: “einen Handel schließen” is to strike a bargain — schließen here is not ‘to shut.’ “dergestalt, daß” is an old formula, ‘in such a way that.’ “wollt” is clipped wollte. The Brabant thaler was a real and rather valuable silver coin, and the exactness of the arithmetic is what the whole tall tale is built on.

sentences.i: Now that I call a good sale!
sentences.n: “heiß” here is the verb heißen in its first-person form, ‘I call,’ not the adjective heiß, ‘hot.’ The line is an aside — the teller stepping in for a moment to admire the bargain.

sentences.t: Der Bauer gieng nun heim, und trug das Maß Rübsamen auf dem Rücken herbei;
sentences.l: The farmer now went home, and carried the measure of rape-seed along on his back;
sentences.n: “gieng” is the 1857 spelling of ging. “herbei” — ‘hither’ — is the particle of herbeitragen, to carry something to where the speaker is.

sentences.t: unterwegs verlor er aber aus dem Sack ein Körnchen.
sentences.l: on the way, however, he lost one little grain out of the sack.
sentences.i: on the way, though, he lost a single little grain out of the sack.
sentences.n: “aber” standing inside the clause is a quiet ‘however,’ not the sentence-opening ‘but.’ The diminutive “Körnchen” makes the loss as small as it can possibly be — which is what the arithmetic that follows needs.

sentences.t: Der Metzger bezahlte ihn wie gehandelt war richtig aus;
sentences.l: The butcher paid him out properly, as had been bargained;
sentences.i: The butcher paid him out in full, just as the deal had been struck;
sentences.n: “bezahlte … aus” is separable auszahlen, ‘to pay out.’ In “wie gehandelt war,” handeln is to bargain or trade, not to act. “richtig” here is ‘duly, correctly.’

sentences.t: hätte der Bauer das Korn nicht verloren, so hätte er einen brabanter Thaler mehr gehabt.
sentences.l: had the farmer not lost the grain, so he would have had one Brabant thaler more.
sentences.i: if the farmer had not lost that grain, he would have had one Brabant thaler more.
sentences.n: Another conditional with no wenn, marked by the fronted verb and the answering “so”: ‘had he not …, then he would have …’

sentences.t: Indessen, wie er wieder des Wegs zurück kam, war aus dem Korn ein Baum gewachsen, der reichte bis an den Himmel.
sentences.l: Meanwhile, as he came back the same way, out of the grain a tree had grown, which reached up to heaven.
sentences.i: Meanwhile, as he came back along the same road, a tree had grown out of that grain, and it reached all the way to heaven.
sentences.n: “des Wegs” is an adverbial genitive, ‘along the way.’ “reichte” here is reichen in the sense ‘to reach, extend,’ not ‘to hand over.’ “Himmel” is both sky and heaven, and the tale is about to use both senses at once.

sentences.t: Da dachte der Bauer „weil die Gelegenheit da ist, mußt du doch sehen, was die Engel da droben machen, und ihnen einmal unter die Augen gucken.“
sentences.l: Then the farmer thought, “since the opportunity is there, you must indeed see what the angels are doing up there, and peer at them once under the eyes.”
sentences.i: Then the farmer thought, “while the chance is here, I may as well see what the angels are up to overhead, and get a look at them face to face.”
sentences.n: He addresses himself as “du,” a very common German way of thinking aloud; English generally turns it into ‘I.’ “jemandem unter die Augen gucken” is to get a close look at someone’s face. “doch” and “einmal” are flavouring particles that no single English word carries.

sentences.t: Also stieg er hinauf und sah daß die Engel oben Hafer droschen und schaute das mit an;
sentences.l: So he climbed up and saw that the angels up above were threshing oats and looked on at it;
sentences.i: So he climbed up and saw that the angels up there were threshing oats, and stood watching;
sentences.n: “mit ansehen” is to look on at something as it happens; the “mit” is the separable particle and stands well away from its verb. Threshing is farm work, and the tale reports heaven as a barn without a flicker.

sentences.t: wie er so schaute, merkte er, daß der Baum, worauf er stand, anfieng zu wackeln, guckte hinunter und sah daß ihn eben einer umhauen wollte.
sentences.l: as he was looking so, he noticed that the tree he stood on began to wobble, looked down and saw that someone was just then about to fell it.
sentences.i: as he stood watching, he noticed that the tree he was standing on had begun to sway, looked down, and saw that someone was in the act of felling it.
sentences.n: “worauf” = wo- + auf, ‘on which’; German prefers this compound to a preposition with a relative pronoun when the thing referred to is not a person. “eben” means ‘just at that moment,’ and “einer” is the indefinite ‘someone.’

sentences.t: „Wenn du da herab stürztest, das wär ein böses Ding“ dachte er, und in der Noth wußt er sich nicht besser zu helfen, als daß er die Spreu vom Hafer nahm, die haufenweis da lag, und daraus einen Strick drehte:
sentences.l: “If you plunged down from there, that would be a bad business,” he thought, and in his distress he knew no better way to help himself than to take the chaff from the oats, which lay there in heaps, and twist a rope out of it:
sentences.i: “If you were to come down from there, that would be a bad business,” he thought, and in his need he could think of nothing better than to take the chaff from the oats, which lay about in heaps, and twist a rope out of it:
sentences.n: “sich zu helfen wissen” — to know how to help oneself, i.e. to see a way out. “wußt” and “wär” are clipped wußte and wäre. “haufenweis” is an adverb, ‘in heaps.’ Chaff is the husk left behind by threshing, so a rope twisted from it would hold nothing whatever; the tale says so without comment, and that is the humour.

sentences.t: auch griff er nach einer Hacke und einem Dreschflegel, die da herum im Himmel lagen, und ließ sich an dem Seil herunter.
sentences.l: he also reached for a mattock and a flail, which lay about there in heaven, and let himself down on the rope.
sentences.i: he also took up a mattock and a flail that were lying about up in heaven, and let himself down by the rope.
sentences.n: “ließ sich … herunter” is separable herunterlassen, ‘to let oneself down.’ The tale simply hands him the two tools its ending will need. What a threshing-flail is doing in heaven has in fact already been answered by the angels at their threshing.

sentences.t: Er kam aber unten auf der Erde gerade in ein tiefes tiefes Loch, und da war es ein rechtes Glück, daß er die Hacke hatte,
sentences.l: But below on the earth he came down right into a deep deep hole, and there it was a real piece of luck that he had the mattock,
sentences.i: But down on the earth he landed right in a deep, deep hole, and there it was a real piece of luck that he had the mattock,
sentences.n: “ein tiefes tiefes Loch,” the adjective doubled with no comma, is a spoken storyteller’s way of deepening the hole. “ein rechtes Glück” is ‘a proper, real piece of luck.’

sentences.t: denn er hackte sich damit eine Treppe, stieg in die Höhe und brachte den Dreschflegel zum Wahrzeichen mit, so daß niemand an seiner Erzählung mehr zweifeln konnte.
sentences.l: for he hacked himself a staircase with it, climbed up into the height and brought the flail along as a token, so that no one could doubt his tale any more.
sentences.i: for he hacked himself a staircase with it, climbed up out, and brought the flail along as proof, so that no one could doubt his tale any longer.
sentences.n: “sich eine Treppe hacken” has the dative “sich,” ‘for himself.’ “zum Wahrzeichen” — as a token, a proof; the object brought back as evidence is a standing device in these tales. “an etwas zweifeln” takes an. The ending is deadpan: the only thing the flail proves is that he has a flail.

glossary.drehte: drehen — twisted, turned (3rd sg. preterite; einen Strick drehen: to twist a rope)
glossary.es: es — it; here chiefly the dummy subject that fills the front slot (Es zog einmal ein Bauer …), which English drops
glossary.gehandelt: handeln — bargained, traded (past participle; wie gehandelt war: as the bargain had been struck); also handeln ‘to act’
glossary.heiß: heißen — call, name (1st sg. present: das heiß ich … = that I call …); also heiß, the adjective ‘hot’
glossary.maß: das Maß — a measure (a fixed quantity of grain or drink: ein Maß Rübsamen); also Maß halten, to keep moderation
glossary.reichte: reichen — reached, extended (3rd sg. preterite; reichte bis an den Himmel: reached up to heaven); also ‘handed, passed’
glossary.schlossen: schließen — struck, concluded (3rd pl. preterite; einen Handel schließen: to strike a bargain); also ‘shut, locked’
glossary.verkauft: verkaufen — sold (past participle; gut verkauft: well sold); also verkauft, 2nd pl. imperative ‘sell’
glossary.wollt: wollen — would, wanted to (3rd sg. preterite, clipped wollte: der wollt ihm aufzählen); also wollt, the 2nd pl. ‘you want’
glossary.zog: ziehen — set out, went (3rd sg. preterite; zog … aus, from ausziehen, to set out); also zog an, ‘put on’
